stem: An adult newly diagnosed with type 2 diabetes says, “My vision is fine, so I don’t think I need an eye examination.” Which response by the nurse is best?

options.A: A dilated comprehensive eye examination is recommended at the time type 2 diabetes is diagnosed because diabetic retinopathy can be present without noticeable vision symptoms.
options.B: Eye screening should begin only after blurred vision or other visual symptoms develop.
options.C: Diabetic retinopathy always causes early pain or obvious visual changes, so symptom monitoring is sufficient.
options.D: Routine eye examination is unnecessary in type 2 diabetes unless the client first develops a foot or kidney complication.

rationale: A is correct. The 2026 ADA Standards of Care recommend that people with type 2 diabetes receive an initial dilated and comprehensive eye examination by an ophthalmologist or optometrist at the time of diabetes diagnosis. Retinopathy may be advanced or vision-threatening while the person remains asymptomatic, so waiting for vision changes can delay detection and treatment. B and C incorrectly rely on symptoms. D adds an unsupported requirement for another complication before eye screening.
educational_objective: Teach adults with newly diagnosed type 2 diabetes that retinopathy screening begins at diagnosis even when vision is normal because clinically important retinal disease may be asymptomatic.
source_organization: American Diabetes Association Professional Practice Committee
source_document_title: Retinopathy, Neuropathy, and Foot Care: Standards of Care in Diabetes—2026
source_locator: Diabetic Retinopathy Screening Recommendation 12.4 — people with type 2 diabetes should have an initial dilated and comprehensive eye examination at diagnosis; screening discussion — vision-threatening retinopathy may be asymptomatic and prompt diagnosis permits timely intervention
source_claim_supported: Type 2 diabetes warrants an initial dilated comprehensive eye examination at diagnosis, and absence of visual symptoms does not exclude clinically important diabetic retinopathy.
blueprint_source_organization: National Council of State Boards of Nursing
blueprint_locator: Health Promotion and Maintenance — reinforce preventive screening and early detection practices for chronic disease complications
blueprint_topic: Health Promotion and Maintenance — diabetic retinopathy screening
correction_summary: Rebuilt the source item because gradual vision change is nonspecific and should not be treated as diagnostic of diabetic retinopathy. The final item tests the directly supported preventive-screening principle that type 2 diabetes requires eye examination at diagnosis even in an asymptomatic client.
audit_reviewer: OpenAI GPT-5.6 Sol — Rule 1 clinical audit + adversarial second pass

audit_findings.source_audit: Verified directly against ADA Standards of Care 2026 Section 12. Recommendation 12.4 provides the exact screening timing and the text explicitly notes that vision-threatening retinopathy may be asymptomatic.
audit_findings.claim_by_claim: A uses the exact population and timing. The rationale avoids diagnosing any current retinal disease in the client and avoids inventing a universal subsequent screening interval.
audit_findings.choice_A: Correct; initial dilated comprehensive examination is recommended at type 2 diabetes diagnosis even without symptoms.
audit_findings.choice_B: Incorrect; waiting for symptoms can miss asymptomatic retinopathy.
audit_findings.choice_C: Incorrect; retinopathy may be asymptomatic rather than painful or obvious early.
audit_findings.choice_D: Incorrect; another microvascular complication is not a prerequisite for retinopathy screening.
audit_findings.ambiguity_second_answer: Only A follows current screening guidance and explains why normal vision does not defer examination.
audit_findings.cueing: All options address the need and timing of screening; the correct choice depends on guideline knowledge.
audit_findings.blueprint: Health Promotion and Maintenance is appropriate because the item tests preventive screening and client education.
audit_findings.independent_adversarial_second_pass: Rechecked type 1 versus type 2 screening timing, symptom nonspecificity, asymptomatic disease, optometrist/ophthalmologist wording, category mapping, and second-answer risk. No unresolved conflict remained.
